newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers voice concern on Haitian reform.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers voice concern on Haitian reform.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers voiced concern on Wednesday about threats to Haiti's political and economic reforms and urged President Rene Preval to renew his commitment to reform in the fragile democracy.
They also urged U.S. President Bill Clinton to pay more attention to Haiti and give more support to its nascent democracy.

Concern over Haiti has risen in the last few weeks. Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resigned in June amid controversy over his plans to privatise portions of the economy and a successor has not been named.
Just days later, run-off Senate elections were postponed amid great acrimony, adding to the uncertainty about the country's direction.

In a bipartisan statement the chairman of the House of Representatives International Relations Committee, Representative Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, and the panel's senior Democrat, Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana, said Haiti had "made progress" since the 1994 restoration of democracy and the return of then-President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who had been exiled after a coup.

"But we fear that if greater efforts are not made in the weeks and months ahead, those gains could be lost," they said in a statement. They called on Preval to "renew his commitment to reforms and to use his office and stature to make the necessary changes to ensure free and fair elections."
Separately, Representative John Conyers of Michigan, the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, and four other members of Congress returned on Wednesday from a fact-finding trip to Haiti.

They acknowledged problems there, but Conyers said both Aristide and Preval had expressed their commitment to resolve the dispute over the Senate elections, and had told the delegation that reports of tensions between them were exaggerated.
Conyers said Judiciary Committee members visited because a key concern had been rebuilding the Haitian police force and establishing a fair and effective judicial system.

He did not say how much extra aid he thought the United States should provide, but said more U.S. assistance was needed in a "brick by brick" effort to develop the poorest nation in the Western hemisphere that was trying to emerge from two centuries of dictatorship.
